newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey Islamists gain respite in battle with army.
newsitem.headline: Turkey Islamists gain respite in battle with army.

text.p: Turkey's ruling Islamists won breathing space on Thursday from an army assault in a struggle with the generals for the hearts and minds of the Moslem but secular nation.

Coalition ally Tansu Ciller pledged to stand by Islamist Prime Minister Necmetin Erbakan, and the army denied it was trying to sponsor individual secularist politicians as alternatives to the government.

Ciller, the deputy prime minister, said her True Path Party (DYP) would have nothing to do with an attempt by her fellow secularists in the opposition to form a shadow government that would unseat Erbakan.

"The DYP is not going to hide behind anyone and take part in action to topple the government," Ciller told a meeting of her MPs. "For today, stability is necessary. There may be alternatives...but they cannot be a guarantee of stability."
The army, the country's most respected institution, is pushing Erbakan hard to curtail a rise in Islamist sentiment in what the generals see as a matter of national survival.

The army pressure has exposed cracks in the coalition. Analysts say government unity is slowly unravelling but that Ciller, due to take over the government next year in a power-sharing deal, will try to stay with Erbakan for now.
"The (government's) life expectancy is anywhere between a few days and a few months," said a Western diplomat. "A few months is probably more realistic," he said.
Ciller, also the foreign minister, was tainted by corruption charges last year which could damage her support at elections.
Her party has been weakened by the resignation of MPs dismayed at her willingness to deal with the Islamists and is in a poor position to negotiate a government overthrow with other secularists.
The opposition, divided by mostly personal feuds, has not risen to a challenge by Erbakan this week for snap elections.
The army said on Thursday it was steering clear of Turkey's turbulent party politics.
"The Turkish armed forces does not cooperate or favour any personality, political party or group," the military said in a statement carried by the state-run Anatolian news agency.
It was reacting to a story in the Sabah newspaper that said the generals wanted Ciller to win a fight for the leadership of the Turkish right so she could then ward off the Islamist challenge.
Erbakan has so far stalled on complying with a list of 18 harsh anti-Islamist measures the army wants carried out.
His Welfare Party is particularly concerned at plans to close Islamic high schools, which could neutralise the next generation of religious activists.

A court sentenced more than 100 members of an Islamist sect to three years in jail on Wednesday, a day after a senior general warned that the anti-Islamist campaign was a question of "life or death" for the republic.
Turkey's army, the second-largest in NATO, has a history of interventions but the top brass are unlikely to stage a coup against Erbakan because of adverse reaction abroad.
The last coup, in 1980, followed years of street fighting between left and right in which some 5,000 people died.
Trade union leaders laid a wreath in Istanbul's main square in memory of 37 people killed at a May Day rally there 20 years ago, witnesses said.
No one was ever charged for the deaths on May Day, 1977, when a gunman fired on protesters from a building above the square. Most of the victims were crushed to death in the resulting stampede.
